from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        self.play(dot.animate.set_color("#FFC300"), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(dot.animate.set_color("#FF5733"), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(dot.animate.set_color("#FFC300"), run_time=0.5)

        path = Line(self.grid['C3'], self.grid['C6'], color="#33FF57")

        self.play(dot.animate.move_to(self.grid['C6']), run_time=2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Mapping Collisions to Geometry", [

            "Bounces map to reflections within a wedge."
        ])

        dashed_line = DashedLine(start=np.array([0, 0, 0]), end=np.array([0, 1, 0]), color="#33FF57")
        
        angle_text = Text("θ = 45°", font_size=24, color=WHITE)

        # Positioning
        self.place_at_grid(c1, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.place_at_grid(c2, 'B3', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.place_at_grid(ray, 'D2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.place_at_grid(dashed_line, 'D3', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.place_at_grid(angle_text, 'F2', scale_factor=0.8)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(c1), FadeIn(c2))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(Write(angle_text))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Mass ratios dictate the wedge angle size.", "As mass grows, reflections trace an arc.", "The arc length corresponds to value Pi."]
        self.setup_layout("The Limit of Mass Ratios", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Graph mass ratio vs speed
        axes = Axes(x_range=[0, 10, 2], y_range=[0, 3, 1], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        axes.scale(0.5)
        curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.sqrt(x) / (1 + np.sqrt(x)), color="#FFFFFF")
        
        graph_group = VGroup(axes, curve)
        self.place_at_grid(graph_group, 'B2', scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Create(graph_group))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Add asymptote line at limit point
        asymptote = DashedLine(start=axes.c2p(0, 1), end=axes.c2p(10, 1), color="#FF5733")
        self.play(Create(asymptote))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF5733")
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Show shrinking gap
        dot = Dot(color=YELLOW).move_to(curve.point_from_proportion(0.9))
        self.play(Indicate(dot))
        self.play(FadeOut(dot))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Collisions track angle in phase space.",
            "Pi emerges from geometric physical constraints.",
            "Blocks act as a physical calculation engine."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Conclusion and Intuition", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FF5733"))
        summary_text = Text("Phase Space: Angle = Arc Length", font_size=28).set_color("#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(summary_text, "B2")
        self.play(Write(summary_text))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#3357FF"))
        box = SurroundingRectangle(Text("Physical Computer: Pi Digits", font_size=32), color="#FFC300", buff=0.2)
        self.place_at_grid(box, "D3")
        self.play(Create(box))
        self.wait(2)
        
        self.play(FadeOut(*self.mobjects))
        self.wait(1)

outline.topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digit Emergence
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate Physics Students or Curious High School Students

sections.title: The Hook: An Unexpected Connection
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive puzzle: How can a series of elastic collisions between two blocks on a frictionless track result in the digits of Pi? Briefly demonstrate the phenomenon visually.
sections.example: A tiny block (mass m) and a large block (mass M = 100^n * m) sliding on a track, where the number of collisions equals the first n digits of Pi.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Establish the foundational rules: Conservation of Momentum and Kinetic Energy in 1D elastic collisions. Use a graphical velocity vector diagram to show how velocities swap or reverse during bounces.
sections.example: A 2D scatter plot showing the 'velocity space'—where the state of the two blocks is a single point moving along an ellipse representing constant energy.

sections.title: Mapping Collisions to Geometry
sections.content: Explain the Galperin billiard-ball transformation. Show how the collision process can be unwrapped into a sequence of reflections of a ray within a circular wedge, effectively turning a 1D collision problem into a 2D geometric arc length problem.
sections.example: Visual animation showing the 'phase space' trajectory bouncing off the circular arc of a unit circle sector.

sections.title: The Limit of Mass Ratios
sections.content: Explain why the mass ratio M/m = 100^n is critical. As the mass of the wall/large block becomes infinite, the angle of the 'bounce' in the phase space approach becomes smaller, approximating the circumference of a circle.
sections.example: An animation of a 'Pac-Man' shaped wedge; as M/m increases, the reflection points trace out the arc length proportional to Pi.

sections.title: Conclusion and Intuition
sections.content: Summarize the 'Physics-to-Math' bridge: Pi emerges because collisions track the angle of a rotating vector in phase space. Encourage students to view complex series through the lens of geometric transformations.
sections.example: A final visual summary: 1 collision = 3, 100 = 31, 10000 = 314. The blocks are essentially acting as a physical computer calculating digits.
